Heaviness
HEV-ee-nes
n.
From heavy + -ness. Renders the Greek lupē, “grief, sorrow,” and katēpheia, “dejection”; and the Hebrew kābēd, “to be heavy.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Heaviness in Scripture is the weighted, oppressed state of the soul under trial, sorrow, or felt withdrawal of God’s ordinary consolations—a real spiritual condition the New Testament names without embarrassment and pastors directly. Peter sets the keynote at 1 Peter 1:6: wherein ye greatly rejoice, though now for a season, if need be, ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations: That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ. Several things stand together in the apostolic teaching. First, the heaviness is real: Peter does not pretend the saints are skipping through their trials; he names the actual weight. Second, it is for a season: the heaviness is not the saint’s permanent condition but a season under God’s appointed providence. Third, it is for trial: the heaviness is the appointed setting in which the faith is proven, refined, found at last unto praise and honor and glory at the appearing of Christ. Fourth, it coexists with deep joy: the same verse says ye greatly rejoice; the joy and the heaviness are simultaneously present, the joy being deep and structural, the heaviness being real and seasonal. Christ Himself entered heaviness in Gethsemane: he began to be sorrowful and very heavy; the writer to the Hebrews encourages saints who are in heaviness through manifold temptations with the example of the Captain of their salvation made perfect through sufferings. The biblical pastoral pattern is therefore not to deny the heaviness, not to pressure the suffering saint into a performed cheerfulness, and not to treat the heaviness as evidence of faithless weakness—but to name it as a real, seasonal, trial-purposed condition that coexists with the deep gospel-grounded joy, and to set the suffering soul under the same providence that brought the same heaviness upon the Christ who has gone through it before him.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines HEAVINESS as the quality of being heavy; weight; in scripture, sadness; sorrow; depression of spirits; affliction—a weighted state of soul under trial that coexists with deep joy.

expand to see more

HEAVINESS, n. — 1. The pressure or weight which any body exerts upon another, in any place near the surface of the earth, by means of the power of gravitation. 2. Sadness; sorrow; grief; depression of spirits. If need be, ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations (1 Pet 1:6). 3. That which is grievous or oppressive.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Peter 1:6-7 — "Wherein ye greatly rejoice, though now for a season, if need be, ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations: That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ."

Matthew 26:37 — "And he took with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, and began to be sorrowful and very heavy."

Romans 9:2 — "That I have great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart."

Isaiah 61:3 — "...to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Heaviness is corrupted, in the contemporary church, by the prosperity-and-cheerfulness register that has trained the believer to perform a constant emotional buoyancy and to read his own heaviness as evidence of faithless weakness—against Peter’s explicit recognition that genuine saints are in heaviness through manifold temptations for a season.

expand to see more

The prosperity-and-cheerfulness register has trained the contemporary believer to perform a constant emotional buoyancy and to read the felt weight of trial as evidence of faithless weakness. The grieving saint is told to just praise through it; the depressed saint is suspected of insufficient gratitude; the heavy season is treated as a problem to be solved by attitude adjustment rather than as a real providence-appointed condition Scripture itself names. Peter refuses this. He writes to saints who are in heaviness through manifold temptations, does not embarrass them with the recognition, and instead frames the heaviness inside the structural deeper joy and the eschatological trial-purpose. The recovery is the recovery of the apostolic candor: real heaviness, named without shame; deep joy, present beneath the heaviness; trial-purpose, framing what God is doing through the season.

Christ Himself entered heaviness, and the Gospel narrative does not embarrass itself with the recognition: he began to be sorrowful and very heavy; my soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death. Paul writes of his great heaviness and continual sorrow for his Jewish kinsmen; Isaiah promises the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness—the trade is real and not the denial of the heaviness. The pastoral application is direct. Honor the heaviness of the saint who is heavy; name it without shame; set it under God’s appointed providence; do not press the sufferer into performance; preach the gospel that holds the deep joy beneath the seasonal weight; wait, with the saint, for the morning that follows the night—and meanwhile know that the same Christ who was heavy in Gethsemane is with the saint who is heavy now, having sanctified the experience by entering it before us.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek lupē (grief, sorrow), katēpheia (dejection), and the verb of Gethsemane adēmoneō (to be deeply distressed); Hebrew kābēd (to be heavy)—the real, seasonal, trial-appointed weight of soul that coexists with deep gospel-grounded joy.

expand to see more

Greek lupē (G3077) — grief, sorrow (1 Pet 1:6 of the saints in heaviness).

Greek adēmoneō (G85) — to be in heaviness, deeply distressed (Matt 26:37 of Christ in Gethsemane).

Greek katēpheia (G2726) — dejection, heaviness (Jas 4:9).

Hebrew kābēd (H3513) — to be heavy, weighty (the cognate of kabod, glory).

Usage

"Heaviness is real, seasonal, trial-appointed, and coexists with the deep gospel-grounded joy beneath it."

"If need be, ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations—Peter names the condition without embarrassment and frames it for trial-purpose."

"Prosperity-and-cheerfulness register pressures the heavy saint into performance; biblical pastoral pattern honors the heaviness and preaches the deeper joy that holds it."
